title: How do we write these four huge totals with powers of ten?
description: Clothing for everyone in the world, honeybees in all the colonies, bacteria in all people, and the seconds spent eating in a lifetime are each found. Every answer is written with one digit before the point, times a power of ten.
teaching_notes: One idea: multiply the numbers in front, add the powers of ten, then move the point so the front number lies between one and ten. Watch for students who multiply the powers instead of adding them.

video_script.why: A product of big numbers is found by multiplying the numbers in front and adding the powers of ten, then moving the point so the front number lies between one and ten.
video_script.substitution: Write each count as a number in front times a power of ten, multiply the front numbers, add the powers, then fix the front number.
video_script.anchor: clothing, honeybees, bacterial cells and eating time for all people
video_script.payoff_line: Multiply the numbers in front, add the powers, then keep the front number between one and ten

final_answer.value: (i) 2.46 × 10 to the power 11 (ii) 5 × 10 to the power 12 (iii) 3.116 × 10 to the power 23 (iv) about 9.198 × 10 to the power 7 seconds
final_answer.spoken: The clothing is two point four six times ten to the power eleven pieces. The bees are five times ten to the power twelve. The bacteria are three point one one six times ten to the power twenty three. Eating takes about nine point one nine eight times ten to the power seven seconds.

maths_rules: (iv) assume 1 hour a day for 70 years: 3600 × 365 × 70 = 91980000 = 9.198 × 10⁷ seconds
check: each front number lies between 1 and 10; the powers were added
video_script.design: Four lines are built one under the other on the working area. The numbers in front are in one colour and the powers of ten in another. A moving point shows each front number being fixed at the answer.
open_questions: The population is taken as 8.2 × 10⁹, the value in the book's list; T12.C2 uses 8 × 10⁹ for a rough sum.
Eating time assumes 1 hour each day for 70 years, as the worklist does; the book gives no figure.

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='cloth'/>Each person in the world has thirty pieces of clothing. How many pieces are there in all?
<bookmark mark='bee'/>There are one hundred million bee colonies, each with about fifty thousand bees. How many bees are there?
<bookmark mark='bact'/>The human body has about thirty eight trillion bacterial cells. How many live in all people together?
<bookmark mark='eat'/>How many seconds does a person spend eating in a lifetime?
<bookmark mark='sci'/>Write each answer using powers of ten.

narration: <bookmark mark='mul'/>Multiply five times ten to the power three by four times ten to the power two.
<bookmark mark='front'/>Multiply the numbers in front, five times four is twenty.
<bookmark mark='pow'/>Add the powers, three plus two is five.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>Twenty has two digits, so move the point one place left and raise the power by one.
<bookmark mark='sci'/>That gives two times ten to the power six. A number with one digit before the point, times a power of ten, is called scientific notation.

narration: <bookmark mark='s3'/>Step three, the bacteria. Thirty eight trillion is three point eight times ten to the power thirteen.
<bookmark mark='f3'/>Multiply the numbers in front, three point eight times eight point two. That is thirty one point one six.
<bookmark mark='p3'/>Add the powers, thirteen plus nine is twenty two.
<bookmark mark='s4'/>Step four, the eating. One hour is three thousand six hundred seconds.
<bookmark mark='mul4'/>Multiply by three hundred sixty five days, then by seventy years. That is ninety one million nine hundred eighty thousand seconds.
